root.note: From qaḍā ‘to judge’. The old Arabic sound ḍ had an l-like quality to Romance ears, which is where the ld comes from.

history: Your town's alcalde was once a judge. Arabic al-qāḍī, ‘the judge’, gave Spanish alcalde. The d is a clue to its age: the Arabic letter ḍ sounded partly like l to early Romance speakers, so they heard -ld-, as in aldea, ‘village’, from aḍ-ḍayʿa. Over time the alcalde changed from a judge to the head of a district, and then to a town's top official. That sense went to America too. Today an alcalde or alcaldesa heads the ayuntamiento, the town hall where you register on the padrón. The other word, cadí, came back into Spanish later for a Muslim judge. So Spanish has the same Arabic word twice.
historyEinfach: Alcalde means ‘mayor’. It comes from Arabic al-qāḍī, ‘the judge’. In the Middle Ages, an alcalde was a judge. Later, the word changed. It came to mean the head of a town. A woman in this job is la alcaldesa. The alcalde's office is in the ayuntamiento, where you go for the padrón.

elsewhere.text: The Spanish mayor is your qāḍī, with a change of job.
Basque has its own form of the word, perhaps through the Tudela area.
In Catalan a mayor is a batlle, and alcalde there is probably a loan from Spanish.
